learningObjective: Determine the degree of shared-memory bank conflict for a stride access pattern and its throughput impact.

canonicalClaims.claim: For a __shared__ float smem[32][32] on Ampere (32 banks × 4 B bank width), a warp-wide access pattern smem[threadIdx.x][fixed_y] produces a 32-way bank conflict because row stride equals the bank period.
conditions: 32 banks × 4 B bank width (default modern compute capability).
No shared-memory padding or swizzling applied.
nonImplications: Does not imply padding to [32][33] is universally optimal; alternative swizzles exist.
Does not imply the kernel is incorrect; only throughput is affected.

misconceptions.claim: The compiler automatically pads shared-memory declarations to avoid conflicts.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Padding must be explicit in source (e.g., [32][33]); the compiler does not silently reshape shared-memory declarations.

misconceptions.claim: Bank conflicts on modern GPUs are limited to half-warp granularity.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Half-warp granularity applied to legacy compute capabilities (Fermi and earlier). Ampere/Hopper use warp-wide conflict analysis.
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: CUDA C++ Programming Guide, compute capability tables

misconceptions.claim: Padding is only needed for double-precision arrays; float arrays are naturally conflict-free.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Conflict depends on the access pattern relative to the bank period, not the element dtype. Both float and double arrays can conflict depending on layout.

implementationFacts: Bank = (byte_address / bank_width) mod num_banks; on Ampere bank_width = 4 B, num_banks = 32.
Padding a 2D array to [dim][dim+1] shifts columns off the periodic alignment and typically resolves conflicts.
Swizzled shared-memory layouts (used in CUTLASS) avoid conflicts without explicit padding.
performanceScenarios: Matrix-transpose kernels are a canonical example of a bank-conflict trap fixed by padding or swizzling.
